But " the typical peak of the season is not until Sept. 10 , and more hurricane activity historically occurs following the peak than prior to it . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content 's credibility : <p> fact-checked <p> proofread <h> Did lawmakers know role of fossil fuels in climate change during Clean Air Act era ? <p> by Christy DeSmith , Harvard Gazette <p> " Today , we think of climate science as different from air pollution , but in the ' 60s , they were very much intertwined , " says co-author Colleen Lanier-Christensen . Credit : Jon Ratner <p> How much was known at the mid-20th century about the dangers of human-caused climate change ? A lot more than most Americans think . <p> In a new paper published in the Ecology Law Quarterly , Naomi Oreskes and a team of science historians detail more than a century of research connecting carbon dioxide emissions with global temperature rise . <p> The findings illuminate what Congress knew , and what it intended , when targeting " air pollution " with the 1970 Clean Air Act , questions that arose during a landmark 2022 Supreme Court ruling limiting the power of federal agencies to enforce @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scientific work that got lost , forgotten , or buried , " said Oreskes , the Henry Charles Lea Professor of the History of Science . <p> Oreskes hopes it will serve as a definitive account of what was understood by the 1950s and ' 60s about the dangers of burning fossil fuels . At 124 pages , the paper surfaces everything from government reports on " inadvertent weather modification " to long-dead lawmakers pondering the future of electric vehicles . It establishes that the era 's experts saw CO2 as one of many environmental threats to regulate . <p> " Today , we think of climate science as different from air pollution , " offered co-author Colleen Lanier-Christensen , Ph.D . ' 23 , a postdoctoral fellow in the History of Science . " But in the ' 60s , they were very much intertwined . " <p> Oreskes started investigating the topic about 10 years ago , originally at the behest of environmental law expert Jody Freeman , the Archibald Cox Professor of Law at Harvard Law School . But the project became all the more urgent with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which restricted the agency 's ability to regulate carbon emissions from power plants , a significant contributor to global warming . <p> The majority opinion , written by Chief Justice John Roberts , relied on " a practical understanding of legislative intent " to find that the authors of the 1970 law would have been more direct had they meant to regulate CO2 . <p> " The Supreme Court was basically posing a historical question , " Lanier-Christensen said . " But then none of the justices actually looked historically at what Congress intended in passing the Clean Air Act . " <p> Irish physicist John Tyndall was the first to describe the heat-trapping effects of greenhouse gases circa 1859 . By the late 19th century , Swedish Nobel laureate chemist Svante Arrhenius had connected atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide to the burning of fossil fuels . In 1896 , he estimated that a doubling of atmospheric CO2 concentrations would warm the planet by 1.5 to 4.5 ? C. <p> In the 1930s , British engineer Guy Stewart Callendar started compiling data on atmospheric CO2 concentrations and global temperatures . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ amounts of coal and oil known to have been burned already . From there , the impact of CO2 on climate was called " The Callendar effect " for several years . <p> American scientists picked up the problem in the 1950s , with physicist Gilbert Plass ' 41 affirming that rising temperatures were connected to human activity . The New York Times covered his research in a 1953 article headlined " How Industry May Change Climate . " <p> By the early 1960s , Callendar was complaining that " everyone likes to ' have a go ' " at the issue . That included a growing community of scientists working in the U.S. government . Central among them was Alvin Weinberg , director of Tennessee 's Oak Ridge National Laboratory . In 1961 , Weinberg spoke to " the deterioration of our atmosphere by the accumulation of CO2 " at a University of Tennessee science fair . <p> And as the decade progressed , an increasing number of ordinary Americans did know . A 1958 documentary by " It 's A Wonderful Life " filmmaker Frank Capra , viewed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , warned that " man may be unwittingly changing the world 's climate through the waste products of his civilization . " <p> Also influential was a February 1969 appearance on " The Merv Griffin Show " by poet Allen Ginsberg . He rattled viewers by claiming that " the current rate of air pollution brought about by the proliferation of automobiles and ' their excrement ' " could cause " the rapid buildup of heat on earth . " <p> In response , one troubled constituent wrote to Sen. Henry " Scoop " Jackson from Washington . The powerful lawmaker ( who twice vied to become the Democratic nominee for president ) forwarded the letter to physicist Lee DuBridge , science adviser to President Richard M. Nixon . <p> DuBridge 's reply to Jackson featured a detailed explanation of increasing CO2 levels and " the greenhouse effect . " By year 's end , DuBridge would revisit these points on the NBC television show " Meet the Press . " <p> Excavating this history sent the paper 's co-authors to a dozen archives . " What makes this challenging @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Environmental Protection Agency existed , " Lanier-Christensen explained . " All functions related to the environment were spread across the federal government . " <p> " You could really see how closely Senator Muskie and his office were following these issues -- from a 1967 report from the secretary of commerce called ' The Automobile and Air Pollution ' to direct correspondence with scientists , " Lanier-Christensen observed . <p> Fast forward to the 21st century , and much of this history has been forgotten , the researchers say . They argue that the U.S. Supreme Court got it wrong with West Virginia v. EPA and note the error also appeared in its 2007 Massachusetts v. EPA decision , which initially granted the EPA authority to regulate CO2 as a pollutant covered under the 1970 Clean Air Act . <p> This was regarded by the court as the unanticipated consequence of an intentionally broad law , with the late Justice John Paul Stevens writing : " When Congress enacted these provisions , the study of climate change was in its infancy . " <p> " When I read that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Oreskes recalled . " It was just so incredibly wrong . " <p> As she tells it , the researchers ' near book-length paper proves without question that CO2 was understood before 1970 as a pollutant as well as a threat to global climate . After all , Muskie introduced the Clean Air Act on the floor of the Senate by warning that unchecked air pollution would continue to " threaten irreversible atmospheric and climatic changes . " <p> But the paper still tells " only the first half of the story , " Oreskes said . A second publication , still in the works , will focus entirely on testimonies to Congress before the legislation was passed , further bolstering the co-authors ' argument that lawmakers had every intention of regulating CO2 . <p> " I do n't expect the justices to read these papers and change their minds , " Oreskes said . " But what they can do is to empower lawyers arguing these cases as they push back against faulty claims . @@113629428 <p> The summer of 2024 was the hottest on record , according to the European Union 's climate monitor , extending an alarming run of temperature records that has put the planet firmly on course to notch its hottest year in human history . <p> The EU 's Copernicus Climate Change Service ( C3S ) said on Friday that the global average temperature for the boreal summer , which refers to the Northern Hemisphere 's June through August period , was the highest on record . <p> The summer months were found to be 0.69 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 average for the June-August period . Effective and efficient taxation and spending can enhance a city , going toward projects that generate revenue to support future projects that draw visitors and contribute to a sense of community for residents . For the world 's most popular destinations , tourism taxes are being increased in an attempt to slow the flow of visitors . @@113754630 <h> Australia has developed a map for getting to net zero -- here 's how it will guide us <p> Australia 's push for net-zero emissions received a welcome boost on Thursday , with the release of an official report showing how Australia can seek to cut domestic emissions across each sector of the economy . <p> The Climate Change Authority prepared the report , which provides vital scaffolding for Australia 's climate ambitions . Hopefully , it will inform the Australian government 's upcoming decarbonization plans for each sector of the economy , and its updated goal for emissions reduction out to 2035 . <p> The pathways laid out by the authority show how emissions cuts can be made in sectors such as land use , resources , transport and energy . Importantly , the report shows what effective climate action looks like -- and what Australia can achieve . <p> The roadmap also shows how Australia can do its part to limit global warming to 1.5 ? C to avoid temperatures climbing dangerously higher . Climate scientists are clear : every fraction of a degree matters . <h> Why are these pathways important ? <p> The authority @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and energy , transport , industry and waste , agriculture and land , built environment , and resources . <p> For each sector of Australia 's economy , getting emissions to net zero poses different challenges and opportunities . <p> Preventing emissions from buildings requires , among other things , getting off gas and making them more efficient . Reducing emissions from transport means encouraging uptake of diverse solutions such as electric vehicles , trains and cycling . <p> The report provides pathways that can guide the decarbonization of each sector . It shows which technologies could be taken up and phased out , how to attract , enable and time investments , and how to align policy with practical implementation . <p> The authority borrows from the approach of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change , by showing a range of possible routes to net zero and comparing their work to others . <p> We hope the Australian government continues this approach , to ensure decision-makers understand how different modeling approaches and scenarios combine to create a robust body of knowledge . <h> Pathways show us the way <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the report just released . Our own sectoral pathways are also designed to support governments , businesses and investors as they look for opportunities to reduce emissions . <p> Why ? Because pathways create a signal of how things can change . Laying out the problem , and different approaches to solving it , helps create a common understanding of the opportunities , risks and barriers to effective action . <p> They make it possible for governments to set clear goals and ensure policies match what is needed and are backed by evidence . Rather than just setting out the overarching intention of , say , cutting emissions in half in a decade , pathways show how it can be done . <p> Pathways let investors and companies identify and reduce risks and get ahead in a global economy aiming for net-zero emissions . <p> And they lay out the technologies and processes needed to make the shift : ranging from mature , ready-to-deploy technologies such as renewable energy and storage , to maturing technologies such as green steelmaking . <h> Pathways to keep 1.5 ? C alive <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ release its new 2035 emissions target , taking us beyond the current target for 2030 . <p> Every signatory to the 2015 Paris Agreement has to publicly set a new target every five years . Other nations are doing the same . <p> In the authority 's plan , Australia would hit net zero by 2040 under the more ambitious pathway aimed at meeting the 1.5 ? C goal , or 2050 under the 2 ? C scenario . These net zero dates are broadly consistent with our own analysis . <p> But there are opportunities to move faster still . <h> Boosted ambitions <p> Transport is now Australia 's fastest-growing source of emissions . The authority 's transport pathway envisages passenger vehicles going electric and encouraging public transport and active transport , such as walking , cycling and micromobility such as e-scooters . <p> It aligns with our research , which shows a diverse solutions approach is a better option to reduce transport emissions . This is especially important given recent delays in the shift to zero-emissions vehicles . <p> However , the authority only takes a diverse approach @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ diversify its approach to freight transport . <p> The authority focuses on moving trucks from diesel and petrol to battery electric and green hydrogen . But Climateworks ' analysis shows we can also reduce distance traveled through route optimization and shift freight to rail , where possible . <p> For the built environment -- our houses , offices and infrastructure -- the report rightly notes most technologies are now technically ready , commercially available , cheaper to run and healthier . They include energy-efficient electrical appliances , roof and wall insulation and window glazing . <p> But there 's an opportunity to go further . <p> The most cost-effective way to green your house depends on which state or territory you live in . Quick fixes -- such as switching gas hot water for heat pumps -- are included in the authority 's report . <p> But as our recent modeling shows , homes in cooler climates benefit from more comprehensive improvements including double-glazing windows and adding insulation to walls and ceilings , alongside the quick fixes . <h> What 's next ? <p> The pathways laid out by the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ left on the shelf . They have very real use for business leaders and investors , as well as for policymakers . <p> These pathways will guide Australia 's comprehensive national net-zero plan . @@113761939 <p> Renault CEO Luca de Meo said today that automakers collectively may need to pay ? 15B in fines if they miss 2025 emissions targets , as they 've failed to ramp up efficient vehicle production in line with EU guidance -- even as consumer EV demand continues to rise in Europe . <p> At issue are Europe 's 2025 CO2 targets , and a penalty calculated based on fleet average CO2 emissions per automaker . <p> By 2025 , automakers are supposed sell vehicles with average emissions of 93.6g/km or lower . If an automaker fails to meet this legal target , which was established in 2017 , it may have to pay a fine of ? 95 per gram of CO2 per car . <p> The potential fines vary by automaker , with some automakers close to meeting the targets and some far away . Multiple automakers have already met the targets , namely Tesla and Volvo , who are well under the requirements . And some are close to meeting them due to high EV or hybrid mix , like Kia , Hyundai and Stellantis . These companies risk a fine of a few hundred euros @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Worst off are Ford and Volkswagen , which have a longer way to go before meeting 2025 targets . These companies could risk fines of ? 2,000+ per car , given their current levels of noncompliance. <h> de Meo tries to avoid blame for fines industry knew were coming <p> Today , Luca de Meo , who is CEO of Renault and also head of the European Automobile Manufacturers Association ( ACEA ) , said to Inter radio in France that fines could total ? 15 billion if fleet emissions remain at today 's level , or that automakers would need to give up the production of 2.5 million polluting vehicles in order to come into compliance . <p> de Meo said " the speed of the electric ramp-up is half of what we would need to achieve the objectives that would allow us not to pay fines , " notably using the words " the electric ramp-up " instead of " our electric ramp-up " in order to suggest blame could come from external factors instead of from the industry itself . <p> de Meo went on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deadlines and fines without being able to make that more flexible is very , very dangerous . " <p> Notably , these targets were established in 2017 , which is more than enough time for automakers to know what they need to do , and were already subject to interim evaluation in 2023 . <p> The average car development cycle is about 7 years long from start to finish , so even if automakers waited until after the 2017 regulation was adopted ( which would have been folly , since both climate change and the necessity of the EV transition have been obvious since well before then ) , they still had plenty of time to bring new models to market that would be ready today . <p> de Meo is n't the only automaker head who has repeatedly called for 11th-hour flexibility on targets they knew about 8 years ahead of time . BMW CEO Oliver Zipse has also called for a review of the targets . <p> But the ACEA , which de Meo is also the head of , says the 2025 targets should remain unchanged , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ time to adapt due to vehicle development and production cycles . " <p> And Transport &amp; Environment , in an April 2024 analysis , showed that these targets are still reachable , just that automakers have put in little effort to reach them yet . <p> In previous years , automakers made the same complaints that new targets would be hard to reach and that they risked fines , begging for leniency instead of just putting in the work needed to meet them . Then , miraculously , when the time came for regulations to go into place , their fleet emissions dropped precipitously from their previous plateau to meet the new targets . It 's almost like the effort was possible all along . I wonder if the same is true here ... <h> Electrek 's Take <p> To be clear : I have absolutely zero sympathy for any automaker who was given years of notice that they would be fined for poisoning the world 's climate , and yet continued to do so and are now asking for lenience . @@113790036 <h> School districts race to invest in cooling solutions as classrooms and playgrounds heat up <p> Ylenia Aguilar raised her two sons in Arizona -- first in Tucson and later Phoenix , so they 're no strangers to scorching heat . Just recently , Phoenix hit its 100th straight day at or above 100 F ( 37.8 C ) , shattering the record set in 1993 . <p> She remembers scary moments " seeing soccer kids and my own children pass out and faint from , you know , heat-related illnesses , " she said . " It was seeing my sons dehydrated . " <p> Scores of U.S. schoolyards like hers are carpeted in heat-absorbing asphalt , with no shade even for play areas . The buildings were often made with wall and roofing materials that radiated heat into indoor spaces . Kids are also more vulnerable to heat illness than adults . Their bodies have a harder time self-regulating in extreme heat in part because they sweat less , so they can become dehydrated faster . Climate change is heightening the risks . School closures related to heat are becoming more frequent , according to a report @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Analytics . <p> There is also accumulating data on temperature inequality and the effects of heat . Low-income neighborhoods and communities of color , which describes Aguilar 's , can be as much as 7 F ( 3.9 C ) hotter than richer and whiter neighborhoods , leaving students and educators to swelter in a warming world . Extreme temperatures also affect learning , performance and concentration . <p> Yet there are well-known ways to cool down schools and neighborhoods . " When the solutions are so at hand and readily available , " said Joe Allen , associate professor and director of the Healthy Buildings program at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health , these conditions are " unacceptable . " <p> In Phoenix , Aguilar became a leader , joining the school board and helping to pass a $50 million bond that funded a number of solutions in her Osborn Elementary School District . <p> Other schools like Aguilar 's are also starting to spend on these fixes . <h> Cool ground surfaces <p> On a hot day in 2022 , students at a school near @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reading of 105 F ( about 40.5 C ) . <p> A roofing manufacturer donated a bright blue , solar-reflective coating and helped them paint it on . They took another reading , this time it was 95 F ( 35 C ) . <p> As students of the private school learned , paved surfaces get really hot in the sun . They absorb solar energy and slowly re-radiate it out as heat , increasing air temperatures by as much as 7 F ( 3.9 C ) . <p> Cooling playgrounds and roads by making them more reflective is not new , but interest has been growing along with more understanding of the way the accumulation can affect entire neighborhoods , known as urban heat islands , said Daniel Metzger , a fellow at Columbia Law School who studies these passive climate adaptation technologies . <p> " And as climate change gets worse ... I think adaptation measures like this are only going to become more and more important , " he said . <p> Workers recently rolled that same cool surface on the parking lot at the Science , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sustainability goals and efforts to minimize heat . Both times , the roofing manufacturer GAF donated the coatings and labor . Without that , the school would have had to raise funds , said Scott Starowicz , the school 's co-founder and chief financial officer . <p> These roofs -- as well as window films , paints and other technologies -- reflect a portion of the incoming solar radiation away from a building , rather than allowing it to transfer into the building as heat . These are some of the easiest and least costly actions a district can take . <p> Experts agree cool roofing does bring down the indoor temperature and reduce the need for AC . Chaffey 's roofs now sit at around 90 F ( 32 C ) . <p> The district has also invested in steel shade structures , trees and thermometers that consider things like temperature and humidity to monitor heat stress . @@113816933 <h> Evaluating own-price dynamics in taxing environmental externalities <p> Irrigation district service area , rate zones , and wells . The service area of the Pajaro Valley Water Management Agency is divided into two different rate zones . The shaded area delineates the Delivered Water Zone , where users began facing a higher water price in 2011 . Each dot represents a groundwater well . The dashed line marks county boundaries ; the service area is split between Santa Cruz County in the north and Monterey County in the south . Credit : Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists ( 2023 ) . DOI : 10.1086/728988 <p> Many parts of the world are experiencing severe drought , and with climate change , many of the planet 's most productive agricultural regions will suffer from increased water scarcity . Agricultural water pricing may be a critical instrument to managing increasingly scarce resources . Thus , understanding agricultural firms ' response to pricing is crucial to deploying prices to regulate water use . <p> The authors of a paper published in the Journal Association of Environmental and Resource Economists quantify the dynamic impacts of pricing groundwater extraction by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pumping to two geographically distinct prices and estimating how farmers respond each year following the price increase . <p> In " The Dynamic Impacts of Pricing Groundwater , " authors Ellen M. Bruno , Katrina K. Jessoe , and W. Michael Hanemann exploit a price shift incurred by a subset of firms that persisted over several years to evaluate how the magnitude of firm response to prices evolves . The research design exploits a legal ruling that exposed some farms in the Pajaro Valley , a productive agricultural area in California , to a large and enduring water price increase . This policy change lends itself to an event study framework to evaluate the water use response in each of the five years following the ruling in a setting characterized by incomplete markets and dwindling supplies . <p> The authors find that average treatment effects obscure important dynamics in firm price response . On average , the 21% price increase reduced groundwater extraction by 22% following the price split . Over time , however , firms become increasingly responsive to prices , with the implied price elasticity doubling between the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Our groundwater results stand in contrast to the convention in the literature that water demand is inelastic , " the authors write . " Over longer time intervals , agricultural groundwater demand is relatively price elastic as farmers adjust through margins that may simply be unavailable in the short run . " <p> The authors note that the work underscores the limitations of using short-run estimates in the design and evaluation of long-run policies . <p> Ultimately , they write , the " difference in price sensitivity over time may be particularly acute in the agricultural water setting given that the available margins of response to farmers within a year -- less irrigation all else equal -- differs substantially from the margins available over a multiyear horizon -- land use decisions . " <p> This document is subject to copyright . Apart from any fair dealing for the purpose of private study or research , no part may be reproduced without the written permission . @@113878927 <h> Study identifies areas of Europe at risk from dengue fever due to spread of Asian tiger mosquito <p> The spread of the Asian tiger mosquito ( Aedes albopictus ) is causing local outbreaks of dengue in Europe . Credit : James Gathany , CDC <p> As Europe grapples with the growing threat of tropical diseases brought by the Asian tiger mosquito , a research breakthrough led by the UK Centre for Ecology &amp; Hydrology ( UKCEH ) is enabling scientists to accurately predict towns across the continent where there is a high risk of dengue fever . <p> Global movement of people , trade and climate change , are now putting half the world 's population at risk of contracting dengue fever . Commonly referred to as the " bone breaker , " the disease may cause severe muscle and joint pain , and in some cases can result in internal bleeding and death . <p> The spread of the Asian tiger mosquito ( Aedes albopictus ) has caused local outbreaks of dengue in France , including Paris , as well as Italy and Spain , spreading the virus by biting returning travelers who were infected while abroad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Scientists expect this invasive mosquito species to eventually gain a foothold in the UK . <h> Improving disease prediction <p> Previous disease risk predictions indicated large regions , such as the whole of southern Europe , had a similar risk of local dengue cases over long timeframes , leaving local authorities uncertain whether their area was likely to be affected and action to prevent outbreaks was necessary . <p> But the UKCEH-led advanced high-resolution modeling divides Europe as well as eastern Asia and North America into 10km squares , providing daily risk assessments for each area . The new research involves a more detailed study of the entire life cycle of a mosquito , examining the impact of local climate and competition for food on species traits such as how long it lives and the number of eggs it lays . This provides more accurate assessments of where , when and for how long there are likely to be local dengue cases . <p> The new modeling has already correctly predicted the locations of several towns that have gone on to have their first dengue outbreaks this year @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in southern France , and Vila-seca , in northeast Spain . <p> Dr. Dominic Brass , an epidemiological modeler at UKCEH , who led the study , says , " We predict that the parts of Europe most affected by dengue fever will continue to be southern France and northern Italy , due to a favorable climate , a stable mosquito population and the high number of travelers returning from tropical countries where the disease is prevalent . <p> " However , areas of risk are expanding northwards . Our ongoing research is modeling the likely extent of future outbreaks in Europe under future climate change . " <p> A map showing the predicted at-risk areas , with the circles showing where outbreaks have occured . Credit : UKCEH <h> Guiding action <p> The study team , from UKCEH , University of Glasgow , University of Reading , and Biomathematics and Statistics Scotland , hopes its more accurate predictions will guide preventative measures in areas that are at risk of dengue outbreaks . Possible action includes checking areas where mosquitoes typically lay their eggs , such as standing water , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advising the public to protect themselves against bites . <p> Study senior author Dr. Steven White of UKCEH says , " Our novel modeling technique shows remarkable accuracy for identifying the seasonal patterns and mechanisms of the risk of dengue fever outbreaks , providing a valuable tool for authorities drawing up action plans to prevent and control the spread of the disease . " <h> Rapid spread <p> In regions where Asian tiger mosquitoes are already established -- including 13 countries in Europe -- it is invaluable to know the times of year when there is greatest risk of a dengue fever outbreak , and how severe the risk is . <p> For other areas , it is useful to know what the disease risk would be if the species did arrive . This change can happen fairly quickly ; Paris , for example , went from the first detection of the tiger mosquito in 2015 to having a dengue outbreak last year . <p> So far , the French capital is the most northerly place in Europe where there has been a local outbreak of dengue fever , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of chikungunya disease in July after someone was bitten by an infected Asian tiger mosquito . <p> The UKCEH researchers say the modeling principles used in the dengue fever study can also be applied to other diseases transmitted by the tiger mosquito , such as chikungunya or Zika . They are currently drawing up risk maps for these diseases . <p> Asian tiger mosquito eggs have been found in south-east England , but the species has not yet become established in the UK . However , the research team warns this is likely to change in the future as the UK feels the effects of climate change . <p> Citation : Study identifies areas of Europe at risk from dengue fever due to spread of Asian tiger mosquito ( 2024 , September 10 ) retrieved 10 September 2024 from https : **39;739;TOOLONG ... @@113878931 <h> The profound impact of COVID-19 on China 's agricultural carbon emissions <p> As global climate warming becomes increasingly severe , scientists are delving deeper into greenhouse gas emissions across various industries . Recently , a study from Duke Kunshan University and Yangzhou University on the changes in China 's agricultural carbon emissions during the COVID-19 pandemic has garnered widespread attention . <p> A study published in the journal Frontiers of Agricultural Science and Engineering systematically calculated the greenhouse gas emissions from agricultural activities in China from 2019 to 2021 , including crop and livestock production , as well as agricultural inputs and energy consumption . The research found that China 's net greenhouse gas emissions ( NGHGE ) from agriculture showed an increasing trend over these three years , with methane ( CH4 ) emissions accounting for the highest proportion , exceeding 65% , primarily due to livestock enteric fermentation and rice cultivation . <h> Methane emissions as the dominant factor <p> According to the study , CH4 emissions played a leading role in the increase in net greenhouse gas emissions during the pandemic . Livestock enteric fermentation and rice cultivation were the main sources of emissions , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ total . <p> The study revealed that in 2019 , the net greenhouse gas emissions from China 's agriculture were 729 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent ( CO2-eq ) , increasing to 740 million tons by 2021 . Although the annual growth rate fluctuated slightly , the overall trend was upward , with a growth rate of 1.34% in 2021 . <p> Changes in the livestock industry during the pandemic were a major factor in the variation of net greenhouse gas emissions . The disruption of the supply chain and reduced demand due to COVID-19 significantly impacted the pig farming industry , leading to a substantial increase in CH4 emissions from manure management . <p> The study found that from 2019 to 2021 , CH4 emissions from pig manure management increased by 26.3% , further rising to 69.2 million tons in 2021 . The contribution of pig manure management to CH4 emissions increased from 75.3% to 81.0% . <h> Nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide emissions <p> In the structure of greenhouse gas emissions , nitrous oxide ( N2O ) and carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) accounted for 22% and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mainly originated from fertilizer application and manure management , with emissions decreasing during the study period . The study highlighted that optimizing fertilizer use and manure management practices is crucial for reducing N2O emissions . <p> CO2 emissions primarily came from diesel use and agricultural electricity consumption , accounting for more than 60% of CO2 emissions . The study showed that CO2 emissions varied across regions due to differences in agricultural inputs and energy usage , underscoring the need for region-specific mitigation measures . For instance , in modern agricultural areas like Jiangsu and Guangdong , CO2 emissions from agricultural electricity usage require special attention . <h> Significant regional emission differences <p> The study results also indicated significant regional differences in China 's agricultural greenhouse gas emissions , leading to varying regional characteristics of net greenhouse gas emissions . Heilongjiang , Hunan , Guangdong , and Sichuan were the regions with the highest NGHGE , concentrated in key agricultural areas in the northeast , central , southern , and southwestern regions . <p> In contrast , the net emissions in less developed agricultural areas in the west and central regions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rice cultivation , had the highest CH4 emissions . The significant contribution of pig manure management to CH4 emissions also reflected the impact of the pig farming industry scale on regional carbon emissions . <h> The potential of soil carbon sequestration <p> In addition to greenhouse gas emissions , the study explored the potential of soil carbon sequestration . The results showed that from 2019 to 2021 , over 6% of agricultural carbon emissions were offset through soil carbon sequestration . Soil carbon sequestration is an important carbon sink in agricultural ecosystems . <p> By increasing soil organic carbon content , it can not only reduce atmospheric CO2 concentrations but also enhance soil fertility and crop yields . The study suggested that practices such as no-till farming , fallowing , and utilizing crop residues and manure resources could further enhance the effectiveness of soil carbon sequestration . <p> For CH4 emissions , optimizing livestock management and rice cultivation methods are key strategies ; for N2O emissions , innovative fertilizer use and manure management practices are essential ; CO2 emissions should focus on energy use in modern agricultural areas , achieving @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ energy . <p> The study highlighted the close link between agricultural greenhouse gas emissions and regional structures in Hunan province , underscoring the urgency of targeted measures . Understanding and addressing these changes is crucial for achieving a low-carbon transition in agriculture , especially in the context of the significant impact of the pandemic on agricultural production , particularly the livestock industry . <p> In conclusion , this study reveals the profound impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on China 's agricultural greenhouse gas emissions , providing scientific guidance for a greener and more resilient agricultural future . It is hoped that through scientific policies and innovative technologies , China 's agriculture can take more solid steps towards greenhouse gas reduction and climate change mitigation . <p> Citation : The profound impact of COVID-19 on China 's agricultural carbon emissions ( 2024 , September 10 ) retrieved 10 September 2024 from https : **39;1659;TOOLONG ... @@113878933 <h> Study offers hope for the resilience of the American lobster fishery <p> According to a study by researchers at William &amp; Mary 's Batten School of Coastal &amp; Marine Sciences , the American lobster may be more resilient to the effects of climate change than expected . For the first time , experiments performed at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science ( VIMS ) have documented how female American lobsters groom their offspring , providing evidence that these behaviors are not significantly impacted by temperature and acidity levels forecasted for Maine 's coastal waters by the end of the century . <p> The findings are published in the journal Marine Ecology Progress Series . <p> Despite being one of the largest commercial fisheries in the U.S. with an annual economic impact of more than $460 million in Maine alone , few studies have documented the reproductive behavior of female American lobsters . With the Gulf of Maine warming faster than nearly any other ocean surface on the planet , it 's important to understand how the effects of climate change will impact the sustainability of the species and the fishery it supports . <p> " Brood grooming by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not been quantitatively recorded before , " said Abigail Sisti , who is completing her Ph.D . in Marine Science at the Batten School and is lead author on the study . " In other crustaceans , these behaviors can have a significant impact on the survival of their offspring . Because the environment supporting the lobster fishery is rapidly changing , we wanted to understand how it might impact the way they care for their offspring . " <p> Female American lobsters can produce thousands of eggs that they hold under their tails for long periods of time , between five to 12 months , as the embryos develop . In other crustaceans , grooming behaviors help clear out parasites , remove dead eggs and facilitate the flow of water carrying oxygen and nutrients through the densely packed egg masses . <p> The study was part of a larger effort to determine how multiple stressors affect the reproductive success of the species . In this study , the researchers were testing whether increases in water temperatures and acidity had an impact on grooming behaviors and embryo survival . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a moonshot approach , " said Rivest , whose seawater aquarium laboratory at VIMS has been specifically designed to control multiple environmental variables over long periods of time . " The conditions of our control group were set to match current conditions in the Gulf of Maine , while our experimental groups corresponded to temperature and pH predictions for the end of the century . " <p> In addition to their research outcomes , Sisti and others produced an educational curriculum to involve students and teachers in the research . The research as well as the lesson plans are documented through a story map produced by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 's Sea Grant and Ocean Acidification Program . <h> Documenting grooming behavior <p> The researchers partnered with officials from Maine 's Department of Marine Resources to secure lobsters from commercial operations for use in the study . They obtained female lobsters at a marketable size with intact legs , which are frequently lost in the wild or when they are caught . In total , they observed the behavior of 24 lobsters for five months , or until @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ daunting task of reviewing dozens of hours of recordings from underwater cameras and documenting the frequency and type of grooming behaviors as well as the overall survival of the embryos . <p> Lobsters in experimental groups experienced temperature increases of 4 degrees Celsius and acidification levels of -0.5 pH from present conditions . Oxygen levels remained constant for all animals to isolate the effects of temperature and acidity . <p> Rivest , Sisti and others expected to observe several different grooming behaviors , and they hypothesized that grooming would increase in response to environmental stressors . <p> " We did observe a number of grooming behaviors that increased in frequency during embryo development , " said Sisti . " However , neither water temperature nor acidification at the levels in our experiments caused significant behavioral changes or impacted embryo survival . This is encouraging because it shows lobsters may be reproductively resilient to forecasted environmental changes . " <p> Three distinct grooming behaviors were observed by the researchers : <p> Tail fanning , where the lobsters elongate and retract their tails . This promotes water movement throughout the eggs . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ called pleopods on their tails to circulate water around and through the egg mass . <p> Pereopod probing , where lobsters use one of their five pereopods , or walking legs , to poke and probe the eggs . This is thought to help remove parasites and dead eggs while jostling the embryos , although excessive probing can damage embryos or completely strip the egg mass . <h> Despite the optimistic outcomes , questions remain <p> The researchers are optimistic about the results of the study for the future of the fishery . However , they caution there are still many other variables to consider . <p> " While this study focused primarily on maternal behavior , future studies will explore other factors like how the embryos themselves are affected over time by different stressors , " said Rivest . " We also want to explore how these factors are impacting the overall well-being of egg-bearing female lobsters as well as conditions that exist in microenvironments frequented by lobsters . " <p> The variables in the study were determined using forecasts for open ocean conditions . However , wild lobsters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that provide cover from predators . There , the conditions may differ dramatically from those in open water . <p> " In our experiments , control temperatures were akin to spring and summertime conditions in the Gulf of Maine , which may have accelerated embryo development . We recommend future experiments explore behavioral changes during winter-time conditions , " said Sisti . <p> While questions remain , these are positive findings for the American lobster . However , they stand in contrast to findings in other crustacean species . <p> " Our results highlight the need for species-specific investigations of behavior and reproduction under climate change conditions , " said Rivest . " Further understanding of how co-occurring environmental factors influence all aspects of reproduction will be essential for predicting and managing the long-term success of the American lobster fishery . " <p> Citation : Study offers hope for the resilience of the American lobster fishery ( 2024 , September 10 ) retrieved 10 September 2024 from https : **39;1741;TOOLONG ... @@113897126 <p> The IndieWire Craft team continues our quest to talk to the filmmakers of the best films of 2024 by expanding our camera surveys to the fall festivals this year , including TIFF . We reached out to cinematographers with movies playing in the Discovery , Centerpiece , Gala , Midnight Madness , Platform , and Special Presentations categories at Toronto this year , and almost 100 directors of photography responded to our survey about which cameras and lenses were chosen for each project , and why creatively they were the right tools for the job . <p> The stories behind the choices that some cinematographers made for these films are enthralling in their own right . Some are extreme circumstances in and of themselves , with films shot on the sly without permission from governmental authorities , shot on the edge of war zones , and shot in volatile environmental conditions . <p> But it 's instructive to look beyond the choices made for logistical and practical concerns . A handful of films shot on glorious 16mm play at TIFF this year , and all of them made that choice for wildly different reasons -- be it to evoke a specific time period and feeling or to invite a sense of immediacy and play , without a rigid set of strictures that could make filmmaking feel flat . <p> The stalwarts that always show up in IndieWire 's camera surveys -- both Sony 's Venice 1 and Venice 2 , variants of the ALEXA Mini , and Cooke S4 's gentle modern glass -- are present in films large and small ; but our TIFF survey definitely saw the largest contingent so far of directors of photography making use of the ALEXA 35 , and a fair few praising the Nostalgic and Soft Nostalgic textures for being great partners in capturing a warmth in the atmosphere and in actors ' performances . <p> Whatever the cameras or lenses used , whatever the scale of the project , it is fascinating to read how **25;2074;TOOLONG and different projects utilize the same equipment to create drastically different looks . Each film has its own perspective , and their directors of photography have now shed light on just how they 've used the tools at their disposal to shape a distinct point of view . <p> Films are listed alphabetically by title . <h> ' Aberdeen ' <p> Jesse Wicklund : ' Aberdeen ' was shot with two formats portraying two different time periods : One in the 1970s and another in the 2020s . We utilized an anamorphic 2.39:1 image capture for the ' 20s and spherical 1.85:1 image capture for the ' 70s . I thought it would be interesting to portray two different eras in a person 's life with aspect ratio and lenses as opposed to color -- which we do lean into , but not in an overly dramatic/distracting way . <p> During the process of finding the look , I tested multiple sets of anamorphic and spherical glass . Eventually we landed on the Master Prime anamorphic and Zeiss supreme radiance spherical lenses . The Master Prime anamorphic allowed us to utilize a clean , sharp image at any stop without having to worry about introducing unwanted characteristics . I wanted to get as close as I could to an image that felt as though we were looking through a window at somebody 's life , and the Master Prime anamorphic lenses allowed us to do that . The Supreme Prime radiance lenses provided a beautiful impressionistic look that was n't overly distracting and still felt grounded in reality , the lushness of those lenses I felt complimented the innocence of our titular character in her adolescence during the ' 70s . <p> These lenses coupled with the ALEXA 35 allowed me immense flexibility with capturing the images that we did with mostly available light . Our film Aberdeen would not have been possible without these tools given our restrictions and tight schedule , I knew I needed tools that were going to help protect me and the final image in post . The speed of the lenses and the dynamic range/color of the ALEXA 35 proved to be a magic combination , and I could n't be more pleased with the results we got . <h> ' Addition ' <p> Gin Loane : I needed a kit that would work well in low light wide open . The superspeeds allowed us to move fast , which is important on a five-week shoot . We could be reactive to whatever natural light was presenting itself and augment to suit . <p> I chose a working LUT that had good contrast and changed the color temperature of the camera and lighting to reflect what was going on in the scenes . We fluctuated between being restrained and observant when Grace is trying her best in the real world and then switching to a more subjective style when hooking into Grace 's struggle with her obsessions . <p> Ranabir Das : I find the ALEXA Mini to be the most flexible camera amongst the top-range cameras . The shoot was primarily hand-held and the Mini seemed like the obvious choice . Coupled with the Cooke s4i 's , we were able to achieve a soft , more filmic look . Large parts of the shoot was at night and we were very happy with the results we got in low light conditions . <h> ' Anora ' <p> Drew Daniels : ' Anora ' is about a sex worker who lives in Brighton Beach , Brooklyn , also known as Little Odessa , so it felt like an obvious choice to shoot the film on vintage Soviet glass . We shot mostly on Kodak 500T and 200T , and we often pushed and pulled the stock 1-2 stops and even used an ARRI flasher to achieve a wintry , soft look . I did whatever I could to get the right feel in the image , which often meant under-exposing the negative and beating it up a bit . Sean and I both love the American independent films of the ' 70s , so we tried to use the tools they would have had during that time period to give it a rougher , but still beautiful look . <h> ' April ' <p> Arseni Khachaturan : Our aim was to create a tactile experience for the audience . We really wanted to see the world through the eyes of our main character and also experience it . When we were scouting for the film , Dea and I would drive across the region where the film was shot : Highways , through endless fields , village roads ... we saw the vast beauty of the place where Nina lives and where she performs clandestine abortions . We wanted to bring the viewers very close to this world . <p> When working with Dea , we usually like to shoot most or the entire film -- with just one lens . This constraint , or a rule , that we establish for ourselves helps to commit to a certain point of view , very specific perspective that we craft throughout the film . We decided to mainly work with natural light . All the night scenes are shot in blue hour . Exteriors in the film consist of shots of bright days and blue nights . The lenses we chose , Master Primes , were good for this reason , as they are fast and allowed us to really push the exposure to the limit without any need for additional lighting . <p> This helped to achieve stark contrast between days and nights -- as Nina is constantly on the move traveling to the homes of her patients or cruising the streets at night looking to pick up strangers for intimate encounters . <h> ' The Assessment ' <p> Magnus Nordenhof J ? nck : When I first read the script and talked it over with Fleur , it was the human drama set within the sci-fi world that I felt attracted to . In between the lines , there was a sense of isolation and loneliness in the characters and in the landscape of the film that was very interesting and somewhat felt like a visual key . The story is set in a future where climate change has destroyed the world as we know it today . It 's about a couple who want to have a child , but they can only do so if they get approval from a state assessor . This forces them -- and the assessor -- to really examine their relationships themselves and question who they are on a deeper level . <p> Choosing the right lenses was about finding a balance between the human intimacy of the story and its sci-fi components . The Summilux lenses felt right . They gave us a modern , contemporary look while offering a soft , almost vintage quality -- without the additional layers that older glass can sometimes introduce . <p> The decision to shoot on the ALEXA Mini was driven by both artistic and practical considerations . Filming in the rugged terrain of Tenerife we needed a camera that could handle natural light , magic hour scenes , a lot of handheld work in confined spaces , strong harsh sunlight with hard shadows and night scenes lit with only practicals . <p> On top of that the ARRI sensor 's ability to capture colors , especially reds and yellows , was important , since those colors were key to the set design . Additionally , my familiarity and trust in the ALEXA system was important , especially with our tight schedule and remote locations . <h> ' Beloved Tropic ' <p> Nicol ? s Wong , CCR : I wanted soft but reliable lenses that were also small and light . Super Speeds were the right choice for they excel with faces and have a smooth focus drop off . They have just the right amount of character while still being fairly faithful to reality . <h> ' Better Man ' <p> Wilson Erik : It was important to make the camera react to the action as instinctively as possible , so having as many eccentricities and flares as these lenses gave us , forced the camera work to be totally in the moment of the scene . I had feared that we would have to shoot the whole movie clean and add visual character later considering the form of the main character , but our genius VFX super and producer from Weta saw our initial lens test with as many flares and aberrations we could possible manage , and fully bought into the visual language we set out to achieve . <p> The same ethos applied to lighting , where we would add practical lights to a set only when needed , and traditional movie lights were used only when recreating natural and practical lighting conditions on a set . <h> ' Bird ' <p> Robbie Ryan : The Zeiss Ultra 16 range of lenses are the sharpest for 16mm , so that is a no-brainer when shooting on 16mm . I like using the zoom , as there was quite a bit of tracking after scooters , so the zoom was a quick way of reframing and giving energy , which is a big factor in Andrea 's filmmaking . <h> ' Bonjour Tristesse ' <p> Maximilian Pittner : Durga and I wanted something timeless but disorienting which informed a lot of the choices we made on lighting , movement , and framing -- especially for the part that plays in the south of France . There was something interesting to me in using the main location in Cassis like a studio and we went for something more stylized for our daytime interiors , which we wanted to feel quite dark compared to the harsh sun and the punchy blue outside , as well as the night exteriors . We went for 1.66:1 as our aspect ratio , which also felt like a fitting frame into a heightened world we wanted to create . <p> For the second part of the movie , which plays in Paris , we changed lenses from Cooke S4 to B&amp;L Super Baltars and muted the look we made together with MELS and colorist J ? r ? me Cloutier to have the image feel more tactile and real . We also used more of the sensor of the ALEXA 35 , which I cropped for the first part to have a slight change in the characters ' perception . <h> ' Boong ' <p> Tanay Satam : Working with the ALEXA and hawk C series was a choice I made based on the narrative of the film . ' Boong ' , being based on a young boy 's journey , I wanted a more simplistic approach to the visual storytelling and the ALEXA is my go-to for when I want the image to feel natural and real . The hawk anamorphics have an old-time quality about them , making them my preferred choice to lend that " stuck in time " essence to the film ( also , I just love shooting anamorphics ) . I wanted the film to feel intimate , personal , and moving all the while , maintaining the childlike intrigue for the audience . <h> ' Bring Them Down ' <p> Nick Cooke : ' Bring Them Down ' was a fast-paced shoot that involved running up and down mountains multiple times , filming all the way . Chris 's favorite lens was a 180mm , and the entire film was shot handheld . So , a lightweight camera package was needed . Ireland in January can be cold and wet , and I was familiar with the ALEXA Mini and wanted the reliability of a tried and tested camera body . Personally , I love the Master Anamorphics , especially when shooting close to wide open . They do n't scream " anamorphic , " yet they have a distinct quality , avoiding the flare that most anamorphic lenses would create with headlights , head torches , and small light sources , which would have been too distracting for most of our scenes . <h> ' Can I Get a Witness ' <p> C. Kim Miles , ASC , CSC , MYSC : There are multiple reasons we chose the ALEXA 35 for the project . I had very early involvement with the camera when it was introduced , and had very much enjoyed using it on a previous movie . The exposure latitude that it offers is unparalleled , and we knew that we could rely on that dynamic range to help mitigate lighting requirements on our limited timeframe and budget . Additionally , the texture files that ARRI offers allowed us to select and bake a nice replication of film grain into the image . The Atlas lenses are favorites of mine , having used them on multiple other projects . The combination of modern resolving power , wide maximum aperture and close minimum focus are paired with beautiful classic anamorphic flare characteristics and falloff really helped drive the narrative of the movie . <p> St ? phane Fontaine : We tested lots of different lenses and eventually picked the Tribe7 ( T Tuning ) . One of Edward 's favorite lens was the 27mm which we ended up using for our close-ups . Combined to some diffusion filters , they had an interesting level of gentle softness . As for the zoom lenses , we used them for some very specific narrative moments . <h> ' The Courageous ' <p> Andi Widmer : The relationship between human ( culture ) and nature plays a central role in the film ' The Courageous ' -- not explicitly but implicitly . The place of action is embedded in a wild , lusty nature , which functions as a reminder of human freedom beyond social conventions . The director and I chose an organic look for this setting . The most powerful tools to create this kind of look are texture and color . I experimented a lot with creating textures with digital sensors . The ALEXA 35 was the first camera that allowed me to easily create the suitable texture in camera directly from the sensor data . That 's why I chose this camera and shot the whole movie with the texture G522 Soft Nostalgic . <p> The main character Jule , a freedom-loving woman and loving mother , acts repeatedly contradictorily and the view of her oscillates between sympathy for her difficult situation and a lack of understanding for her actions . It was important to us not to expose her to rejection . That 's why we opted for a soft , warm image . To create this , I chose the Cooke Panchro Classic lenses . They have a soft sharpness , are pleasantly warm and their bokeh is finely divided and differentiated , making the foliage of the omnipresent trees tangible without playing it into the foreground . The wind , which blows often and strongly in the Lower Valais , where we shot the movie , has played its part in the strong presence of nature . However , this is a happy coincidence for the film and not a deliberate choice . <h> ' Crocodile Tears ' <p> Teck Siang Lim : ' Crocodile Tears ' centers on the relationship between a mother and her teenage son , who live in a forgotten crocodile park , now just a shadow of its former self . The real locations of Jonggol and Cikarang inspired director Tumpal to write the script , making it essential for us to capture the textures and the passage of time these places represent . After careful consideration , we chose the 2.39:1 aspect ratio to best convey the connections between our characters , the crocodiles , and their environment . <p> Tumpal drew inspiration from Andrew Wyeth 's paintings for texture and from the eerie , atmospheric lighting in the works of Ben McLaughlin and Thijmen van Kooij for the surreal night scenes . This emphasis on texture and atmosphere led us to opt for large-format cinematography to fully utilize the image sensor and capture these details for the big screen . The choice of anamorphic lenses was crucial , and we selected the Cooke 1.8x FF anamorphic lenses for their warm contrast and minimal distortion , which are often issues with most S35mm anamorphic lenses . These lenses allowed us to frame our characters without distortion while providing a pleasant softness at the edges when shooting with a wide aperture . This created the surreal and organic look we envisioned for the film . <p> Shooting almost wide open during the night scenes further transformed the locations , adding a layer of surrealism . The lack of close focus introduced a sense of space between the camera and our characters , which supported our approach to filmmaking , giving the actors freedom in their blocking . <p> Given the vast range of Southeast Asian skin tones , it was crucial to accurately represent our actors ' skin tones , reflecting their social background , occupations , and origins in the film . The warm contrast of the Cooke optics beautifully captured the delicate nuances of these varying skin tones . <p> Sean Ellis : The film takes place in the present and the past . 16mm black and white was used to show the boxer 's past while 35mm 4 perf anamorphic was used to show his present plight . <p> Much of the film takes place in a hotel room in Las Vegas and with only a 25 day shooting schedule , it was important to move fast . The Cooke 18-100 zoom was converted into a 36-200mm anamorphic zoom and sat on the camera 80% of the time . This enabled us to do quick size changes and also zoom within a take to give the shot a sense of movement . <p> Kodak stocks 7203 , 5203 , 5213 and 5219 were used and flashed with an ARRI Varicon . Cinelab U.K. provided the dailies and deliverables in 4K . <h> ' Diciannove ' <p> Massimiliano Kuveiller : The Supreme Prime T 1.5 lenses were the perfect choice for our film . These lenses allowed us to achieve very sharp and clear images , capturing even the most subtle nuances of emotions in each scene . The large T 1.5 aperture was particularly useful in low-light conditions , helping to create an intimate and evocative atmosphere that reflected the character 's inner world . <p> The lenses maintained consistent quality in all shots , from close-ups that highlighted the protagonist 's expressions to wider angles that situated the character within the environment , ensuring a uniform and coherent look throughout the film . This made it easier to visually connect the scenes in a natural and fluid way . <p> Additionally , the Supreme Prime lenses offered natural color rendering and minimized distortion , giving the film a realistic yet elegant appearance . This visual quality enhanced the emotional impact of the story , making it more engaging . The Supreme Prime T 1.5 lenses provided the quality and flexibility needed to effectively tell the story in a visually captivating way . <h> ' Do I Know You From Somewhere ? ' <p> Lance Kenneth Blakney : In terms of balancing the price point and visual quality , the Blackmagic Design Ursa Mini Pro 12K , combined with various PL Rokinon Xeen prime lenses , ended up being the perfect match to achieve my desired feel for the film . I aimed to create a look that was n't rooted in a crisp , modern style . <p> When telling a story with elements of magic realism , I believe it is important to create a world that supports optical escapism . Combining the lenses with Tiffen Pro-Mist filters ( along with a couple of inexpensive glass prisms to help keep our VFX in-camera ) allowed the visual language of the film to be clearly established , which subtly guides the audience through the inter-dimensional story unfolding in front of them . <h> ' Do n't Cry , Butterfly ' <p> Nghia Ngo Minh : For me , to make a good film , it 's really important for everyone in crew to find the best way to work together . And for my role as cinematographer , after shooting many shorts , series , and feature films , I understood what would be a good fit for this shoot . I needed something small but solid , powerful , handy , and , most importantly , something that would n't go over the budget for shooting and post-production . The Canon EOS camera was the right fit , since Linh and I had used the EOS C700 before in our short film ' Sweet and Salty . ' The C70 is newer and nailed what we needed it to do ; I 'm really happy that I chose it . <p> The challenge was that it 's a digital camera so basically when we took it out with a new lens , everything would be sharp and have a " digital " look ; that 's not the best for my style . The film 's story takes place everywhere in Vietnam , so I had to adjust this digital camera to bring out all the lively imagery over the course of a 28-day shoot with many tiny locations . We chose a set of Lomo Superspeed CKBK Modernized T1.3 . They 're fast , light , and we shot most of the film with the 28mm , which is an unusual focal length for us but it turned out to be a really amazing , light , and powerful combo with the Canon C70 . Julia Simon/NPR hide caption <p> FRENCHMANS BAYOU , Ark. -- Will Tipton 's farm , not far from the Mississippi River , has been in his family since 1836 . For the past eight generations , his family mostly planted one crop per field per year -- and that was it . " Straight soybean , soybean , soybean , " Tipton says . <p> In recent years , Tipton 's been trying something new . He leans over the field and picks up a mass of green leaves . " This is definitely a turnip , " he says , and then picks up a white flowering vegetable . " Daikon radish out here as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crops . Tipton now plants them instead of letting his fields lie fallow after the harvest . Tipton lets some soil come apart in his hands . Eyring is second counselor ) . <p> Nelson , who became a renowned heart surgeon , and Oaks , a former Utah Supreme Court justice , even were called to the Mormon apostleship on the same day in 1984 , but the former was ordained about a month earlier . <p> As such , the 85-year-old Oaks , a former president of LDS Church-owned Brigham Young University and next in line to succeed the 93-year-old Nelson , is well prepared after @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Twelve Apostles . <p> " The interesting thing about Oaks is that he comes from an academic legal background , " said LDS historian Matthew Bowman , author of " The Mormon People : The Making of an American Faith . " " That has made him sort of the point man in church leadership for complex issues of the law . <p> Indeed , unlike Nelson 's immediate predecessors , Thomas S. Monson and Gordon B. Before his apostolic appointment , Oaks already had built a legacy and reputation as a professor , attorney and jurist possessed of a keen , deliberative legal mind . <h> From human laws to God 's laws <p> He clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Justice Earl Warren in 1957-58 and practiced law in Illinois before accepting a professorship at the University of Chicago Law School in 1961 . In 1969 , while heading the school 's discipline committee as it addressed a campus sit-in , Oaks was assaulted twice . <p> He became president of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ J. Reuben Clark Law School . He left BYU in 1980 to join the Utah Supreme Court , where he served as a justice for four years before becoming an apostle . <p> Oaks penned respected scholarly pieces on Fourth Amendment and related issues regarding evidence exclusion . He even delved into whether LDS founder Joseph Smith 's 1844 order to destroy the press of the anti-Mormon Nauvoo Expositor was legal . <p> Oaks opined that while destruction of the printing press itself was illegal , it probably fell within the laws of the time to declare the newspaper 's attacks on Smith as " libelous " and therefore close it down as a " public nuisance . " Either way , the move set the stage for Smith 's assassination three weeks later . <p> While serving on Utah 's high court , Oaks crafted several major opinions . In one case ( KUTV v. Conder ) he wrote a ruling that overturned a lower court 's order barring the news media from using the term " Sugarhouse Rapist " or disclosing past convictions of a defendant during a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vs . Children 's Aid Society of Utah ) Oaks wrote the opinion upholding as constitutional a statute that terminated parental rights of unwed fathers . That case involved a father of an adopted newborn who had failed to file paternity papers within statutory time limits . <p> Former Utah Supreme Court Chief Justice Gordon R. Hall remembered Oaks both as " a first-class member of our court and a real asset " as well as a " good friend . @@114000920 <p> Scientists in Germany have developed a method to obtain protein and vitamin B9 from microbes by providing them with little more than hydrogen , oxygen , and carbon dioxide . <p> Powered by renewable energy , this technology produces a sustainable , nutrient-rich protein substitute that could eventually become a part of our daily diets . <p> " This is a fermentation process similar to how you make beer , but instead of giving the microbes sugar , we gave them gas and acetate , " says author Largus Angenent of the University of T ? bingen , Germany . <p> " We knew that yeast could produce vitamin B9 on their own with sugar , however , we did n't know if they could do the same with acetate . " <h> Yeast , hydrogen , carbon dioxide : A winning combo <p> The researchers developed a bioreactor system with two stages that creates protein- and vitamin B9-rich yeast . In the first stage , a bacterium called Thermoanaerobacter kivui converts hydrogen and carbon dioxide into acetate , a compound also found in vinegar . <p> In the second stage , Saccharomyces cerevisiae ( commonly known as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ generate both protein and vitamin B9 . The hydrogen and oxygen needed for this process can be obtained by splitting water using electricity from renewable sources like wind energy . <p> Interestingly , yeast fed with acetate produces roughly the same amount of vitamin B9 as yeast that relies on sugar . A small portion -- just 6 grams or 0.4 tablespoons of dried yeast -- provides enough vitamin B9 to meet the daily recommended intake . <p> " We are approaching 10 billion people in the world , and with climate change and limited land resources , producing enough food will become harder and harder , " says Angenent . <p> " One alternative is growing proteins in bioreactors through biotechnology rather than growing crops to feed animals . It makes agriculture much more efficient . " <h> Surpassing animal-derived protein <p> The researchers discovered that the protein content in their yeast surpasses that of common sources like beef , pork , fish , and lentils . A serving of 85 grams , or about 6 tablespoons , provides 61% of daily protein needs . Even after treatment , the yeast still delivers 41% of the daily protein requirement , making it a competitive alternative to traditional protein sources . <p> This innovative technology tackles critical global issues such as environmental sustainability , food security , and public health . The system significantly reduces carbon emissions associated with food production by using renewable energy and carbon dioxide . <p> It also breaks the dependence on land for farming , creating opportunities for land conservation . The lead researcher , Angenent , emphasizes that the goal is n't to replace farmers but to encourage the sustainable production of vegetables and crops . The team 's yeast could also be a valuable tool in combating food shortages and nutrient deficiencies , particularly in developing countries . <h> Next steps <p> However , before you can expect to see the team 's yeast on grocery shelves as a protein alternative , lead researcher Angenent notes that there 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and expand production , ensure food safety , perform technical and economic evaluations , and assess consumer demand in the marketplace . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> " The fact that we can make vitamins and protein at the same time at a pretty high production rate without using any land is exciting , " says Angenent . @@114000922 <p> A groundbreaking wildfire detector shaped like a pinecone , made from wax and charcoal , has earned the prestigious UK James Dyson Award . <p> Named Pyri , this device stands out for its unique design inspired by nature and its use of organic materials . <p> The invention , created by students and graduates , has the potential to transform wildfire detection , especially in remote and resource-scarce areas . <h> Pyri 's nature-inspired design and Functionality <p> The design of Pyri is based on pinecones from trees in wildfire-prone regions , where the heat of fires triggers seed release . Similarly , Pyri uses fire to activate its alert system . When a wildfire occurs , the heat melts Pyri 's wax shell , which then releases a saltwater solution . <p> This solution , rich in electrolytes , activates the internal electronics of the device , sending out a radio frequency signal to nearby communities . This simple yet innovative approach allows Pyri to detect and communicate wildfire danger effectively , without relying on traditional sensors , cameras , or satellites . <p> The name " Pyri " refers to the natural phenomenon of " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their seeds when exposed to high temperatures . Pyri mimics this biological response , offering a novel solution to wildfire detection that is not only low-cost but also environmentally friendly . <p> Pyri 's creators , a group of four students from the Royal College of Art and Imperial College London , were inspired by nature to craft a device that works harmoniously with the environment . Richard Alexandre , one of the team members , was particularly motivated after witnessing the devastation caused by wildfires in Brazil 's Pantanal wetlands in 2020 . <p> " There genuinely are no similar ideas or concepts on the market to Pyri , " Alexandre shared in an interview with Dezeen . " Unlike traditional methods , which rely heavily on sensors , cameras and satellites -- often limited by coverage , accuracy , and high costs -- Pyri offers an effective , affordable solution suitable for extensive deployment , even in remote locations . " <h> Affordable , low-maintenance , and eco-friendly <p> One of Pyri 's standout features is its simplicity . The device is low-cost , easy to install , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for large , remote areas prone to wildfires . Pyri can be deployed by helicopter , enabling the coverage of vast areas in a single day . This efficiency in deployment offers significant advantages over traditional wildfire detection methods . <p> The wax serves as a natural trigger , eliminating the need for a conventional sensor , while charcoal acts as an electrical conductor . <p> " These materials were chosen for their abundance , effectiveness , and non-toxicity to the environment compared to conventional materials like plastic and toxic metals like lithium and cobalt in batteries , " Alexandre explained . <p> In the event of a fire , the wax shell melts , triggering the electronics inside to send a signal via a charcoal composite antenna . This signal can be picked up by communication towers or receivers located tens of kilometers away . <p> Pyri uses minimal amounts of metal , only where absolutely necessary , with a focus on abundant and non-toxic materials like aluminum . If the device is never activated , it remains in the environment as a harmless , non-toxic object . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ device is still in development . The team has successfully tested each component individually , but they are now working towards integrating everything into a fully functioning prototype . Once completed , this prototype will be tested in controlled fire environments to ensure its effectiveness in real-world wildfire scenarios . <h> Future development and international competition <p> The James Dyson Award win provides the Pyri team with ? 5,000 to advance their work and develop a fully functional prototype . They are also competing for the $37,000 ( ? 30,000 ) grand prize in the international leg of the competition , where they face 29 other country-level winners . Winning this global prize would offer additional resources for further development and large-scale deployment . <p> As wildfires increase in frequency due to climate change , devices like Pyri could play a crucial role in reducing their impact . Alexandre and his team are committed to continuing their research and development , driven by the urgent need for more effective wildfire detection solutions . <p> In addition to Pyri , other wildfire detection innovations are also emerging . In 2023 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Turkey for its contribution to detecting and managing wildfires . As more solutions like Pyri and ForestGuard are developed , the future of wildfire detection looks promising . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> 0COMMENT <p> NEWSLETTER <h> The Blueprint Daily <p> Stay up-to-date on engineering , tech , space , and science news with The Blueprint .
